albums.blurb: Azymuth are a Rio de Janeiro trio — José Roberto Bertrami on keyboards, Alex Malheiros on bass and Ivan Conti on drums — who described their blend of samba, jazz and funk as "samba doido" (crazy samba). Light as a Feather was their 1979 debut for the American jazz label Milestone and the record that carried them to an international audience, all Fender Rhodes, analog synths and samba-rooted grooves, capped by the nine-minute spacey dancefloor cut "Jazz Carnival".
albums.reception: Its single "Jazz Carnival" became a surprise overseas hit, reaching No. 19 on the UK Singles Chart in early 1980.

albums.blurb: The second album from the London singer and guitarist, released on Warner Bros. three years after her debut Is Your Love Big Enough?. It grew out of a trip to Jamaica, where her mother's family is from, and folds that heritage into a fuller, groove-leaning soul sound than the sparse guitar settings of the debut, led by the singles "Unstoppable" and "What You Don't Do".
albums.reception: Blood entered the UK Albums Chart at No. 2 — still her career-best chart position — and drew generally favorable reviews, with a Metacritic score of 72.

albums.blurb: The second album by the Tokyo trio of Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi, built on synthesizers and sequencers at a time when almost no pop records were. It holds their signature pieces "Technopolis", "Rydeen" and "Behind the Mask" — the last later given new lyrics and recorded by Michael Jackson and covered by Eric Clapton — and it helped set the template for the synth-pop, techno and video-game music that followed.
albums.reception: It topped Japan's Oricon album chart, sold over a million copies to become the country's best-selling album of 1980, and won Best Album at the 1980 Japan Record Awards.
